name: Neckmaxxing / neck training

lead: Neckmaxxing is training the neck muscles to make the neck thicker, which proponents say gives a more masculine, dominant look and better balance between the head, jaw and body. It is described on looksmax.org as a softmaxx.

Neck exercises load the muscles around the cervical spine, with the sternocleidomastoid named in forum guides as the muscle that thickens the neck from the front. Forum posts offer ratio targets, such as neck width to bigonial (jaw) width near 1:1 or a neck-to-height ratio near 1.35, and say a wider neck makes a narrow head and jaw look more in proportion. These are community conventions; no published study validates them and no clinical studies of neck training for appearance were found.

paras: People follow forum guides using neck curls, extensions and similar loaded movements added to a lifting routine, and track neck width with a tape. A thicker neck builds over months of consistent training.
Loaded neck exercises sit near the cervical spine, and one forum guide calls neck work one of the most dangerous softmaxxes. Gradual loading and careful form are the usual precautions in guides.

web.title: How to get a thicker neck - Healthline

angle.text: Neckmaxxers train the neck to make it thicker, which they say adds a masculine, dominant look and better face and frame proportions. A wider neck sits more in balance with the jaw and shoulders. Neck-to-jaw ratio targets circulate on forums, and no published study validates them.

lead: Neckmaxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of training the neck muscles to build a thicker, more defined neck. Practitioners say a wider neck gives the head and jaw a stronger frame, adds to a masculine, powerful look and balances a broad jaw or shoulders, and forum members describe it as one of the more visible changes available from lifting.[1][2][3] The term sits within softmaxxing, the non-invasive branch of looksmaxxing that also covers skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness.[4]

Forum guides describe neck curls, extensions and side raises, sometimes with a towel or a weight plate, plus slow bodyweight variations that emphasise stretch.[3][5] Community posts give proportion targets: a neck-to-bigonial (jaw width) ratio of about 0.95 to 1, a neck matching the widest part of the face, and in one thread a neck width-to-height ratio near 1.35.[1][2] These are community conventions rather than published standards.

Outside looksmaxxing, neck strengthening is studied in sport and rehabilitation. A randomised trial in healthy women found that ten weeks of neck training increased the cross-sectional area of the neck muscles, with larger gains when resistance work was combined with proprioceptive exercises.[6] Consumer health writing also lists flexion, extension, lateral flexion and rotation exercises and says a muscular neck looks strong, especially when flexed.[7]

paras: Neckmaxxing means deliberately adding size and strength to the neck, usually through resistance exercises added to a lifting routine. The aim is visual: forum authors argue that a thin neck under a wide face or a strong jawline breaks the line from head to shoulders, and that a thicker neck restores it.[8] One looksmax.org thread title makes the case that people who have a wider face and better jawline but still a thin neck should train it.[8]

Forum guides describe neck curls, extensions and side raises. One author calls the neck among the most dangerous yet rewarding softmaxxes and claims it could add about 0.5 PSL points.[2] PSL is a community rating scale for looks and is not a validated measure.[4] A thread titled as a guide lists the benefits as a thicker and stronger neck that can go with the physique, improved posture over time and what the author calls a 'high T' look; it demonstrates two exercises done with a towel over the head to avoid a dent from the weight.[3] Replies suggest that slow tempo and a focus on stretch can produce growth even without added weight.[3]

The neck's visible bulk comes from several muscle groups. The sternocleidomastoid is one of the largest and most superficial neck muscles, running obliquely from the sternum and collarbone to the skull behind the ear; it flexes the neck, turns the head and shows clearly when the head rotates.[9] Wikipedia's neck article lists the sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, splenius capitis, levator scapulae and scalene muscles in the posterior triangle, and describes the sternocleidomastoid as the most prominent lateral landmark of the neck.[10]

The same article reports average neck circumferences of about 38.7 cm in men and 33.3 cm in women and attributes the difference mainly to muscle mass, body composition and testosterone.[10] Looksmaxxing posts connect this to the idea of a neck as a sex-linked frame trait, which is the basis of the 'high T' language in some guides.[3]

The randomised pilot trial in healthy women measured three groups of neck muscle: the sternocleidomastoids; the multifidus and semispinalis cervicis; and the semispinalis capitis and splenius muscles. This anatomical breakdown is the closest published analogue to the front, side and back neck work discussed in forum guides.[6]

Posters compare necks to celebrity examples and discuss proportions with the head and jaw, saying that people with a small or narrow skull may already be proportional while those with a wide skull would need to build neck size.[1] A guide on the sternocleidomastoid describes keeping the neck 'packed' during curls.[2] Before and after posts show results of neck training alongside other changes. Threads with titles such as neck training for better looks, neck training jaw area pictures, neck training routine and neck training results show the topic recurring across several years of looksmax.org posts.[11][12][13][14]

Common questions on looksmax.org include how often to train, whether training one side more will leave the neck asymmetrical, how to choose between high and low repetition ranges, and what to change when two months of training shows no results.[5][15][16] One poster started a thread about regaining neck gains before summer, illustrating that members treat neck size as something that can be lost and rebuilt with training.[17]

Forum guides name neck curls and 'neck ups' for the front, extensions for the back, and side raises, using a towel, plate or bodyweight.[3][5] Healthline's guide to a thicker neck lists neck flexion, lateral flexion, extension and rotation, plus shoulder blade squeezes and dumbbell shrugs, and says to rest between sessions rather than training the neck every day.[7]
An electromyographic study in healthy controls compared neck conditioning exercises, providing muscle-activation data on exercises of the kind that appear in looksmaxxing guides.[18]

Community posts give a neck-to-bigonial ratio of about 0.95 to 1 as a target and in one thread a neck width-to-height ratio near 1.35.[1][2] No published study validates these numbers as attractive or ideal.[4]

Looksmaxxing as a term emerged from the PSL forums of the 2010s and spread to TikTok in the early 2020s, with softmaxxing as the name for non-invasive practices including fitness.[4] Neck work as a bodybuilding and combat-sport staple predates this: Wikipedia's neck article notes the neck is highly functional and subject to considerable stress, and sports medicine has long studied neck strengthening in contact sports, aviation and rehabilitation.[10][19] A 1998 military study examined neck training and neck pain in aircrew exposed to high G forces.[19]

On looksmax.org the topic appears in threads of many ages, from short question threads to guide threads and progress photo posts.[1][3][11] No published account traces who first used the specific term neckmaxxing.

A ten-week randomised pilot trial in 26 healthy women reported neck muscle cross-sectional area increases in all three muscle groups measured, between 1.5 and 12.9 percent in a resistance-only group and 18.9 to 32.3 percent in a resistance plus proprioceptive group. Strength gains did not differ significantly between the groups.[6] A randomised study of 180 women with chronic neck pain found that neck strength rose most in a high-intensity isometric group, with the greatest gains in the first two months and improvement continuing up to 12 months.[20]

In sports medicine, a systematic review and expert Delphi consensus examined neck training to reduce head acceleration events in collision, combat and motor sport, with 18 international experts taking part in the consensus stage.[21] A 2024 study in college athletes examined a simple cervical spine exercise regimen and concussion rates, and a 2025 systematic review of purposeful headers in soccer discusses factors that influence head acceleration.[22][23] A trial using transcranial magnetic stimulation reported that specific neck training increased motor evoked potential amplitudes by 67 percent for up to seven days, a neural rather than visual effect.[24][25]

Healthline's guide to a thicker neck says that visible results can appear within weeks to months depending on fitness, body size and body fat, and that neck exercises can ease tension and help prevent injury.[7] Wikipedia notes that men's greater neck circumference is mostly due to muscle mass, body composition and testosterone.[10] None of these sources studies neck width as a factor in rated attractiveness.

Healthline advises stopping any neck exercise that causes pain, moving slowly with good posture, and speaking to a doctor before starting a new programme; it says overworking or misusing neck muscles can cause pain or injury.[7] A looksmax.org guide itself calls neck work one of the most dangerous softmaxxes.[2]

One looksmax.org thread title raises the possibility that neck training can cause sleep apnoea.[26] Healthline notes that excess neck fat, often associated with obesity, is linked to narrower airways and higher sleep apnoea risk, and distinguishes a thick neck from a large neck due to Cushing syndrome; it also notes that larger neck circumference has been associated with cardiometabolic risk in a 2010 study.[7][10]

No studies found of neck training for facial or physique appearance in the looksmaxxing sense. Related studies of neck training include a randomised pilot trial measuring neck muscle size after resistance and proprioceptive training,[6] a 12-month randomised study of strength training for chronic neck pain,[20] a Delphi consensus on neck training in sport,[21] an electromyographic comparison of neck conditioning exercises,[18] a preliminary study of neck training and neck pain in high-G aircrew,[19] and trials of corticomotor effects of neck training.[24][25]

Neckmaxxing is usually presented as a low-cost, equipment-light softmaxx that can be done alongside regular lifting, and as a counterpart to jaw and shoulder work.[2][3][8] Some posters describe it as 'lifefuel', a community term for a motivating, positive practice.[14] Others raise questions about asymmetry and slow progress, which the threads answer with practical suggestions about training both sides and adding tension.[5][15]

lore.intro: Neckmaxxing threads on looksmax.org mix anatomy, ratio targets, training guides and progress photos, and a few raise safety questions.[1][2][5][26]

claims.claim: A neck about as wide as the jaw is ideal.
Neck training can add notable rating points to overall looks.
Neck muscles respond to training and can be built.
A thick neck goes with a high-testosterone look and better posture.
You can build the neck with bodyweight and slow tempo, without added weight.
Training one side more will make the neck asymmetrical.
Neck training is risky or can cause sleep apnoea.

timeline.event: A military study examines neck training and neck pain in aircrew exposed to high G forces.[19]
A randomised study of 180 women with chronic neck pain reports strength gains lasting up to 12 months after neck training.[20]
An electromyographic comparison of neck conditioning exercises in healthy controls is published.[18]
A study associates larger neck circumference with cardiometabolic risk, as noted in consumer health writing.[7]
A randomised pilot trial in healthy women reports neck muscle cross-sectional area gains after ten weeks, and a separate trial reports corticomotor changes after specific neck training.[6][24]
Looksmaxxing spreads to TikTok, bringing softmaxxing practices to a wider audience.[4]
A study of a cervical spine exercise regimen in college athletes and concussion rates is published.[22]
A systematic review and Delphi consensus on neck training to reduce head acceleration events in sport is published.[21]
